queries.hook: When the darkness feels endless and the heart is too tired to go on, and no one seems to see the pain.
queries.diagnose: Fear grows from imagining the future and from forgetting that what is real in us cannot be lost; worry multiplies what has not happened.
queries.steady: This darkness is a passing night, not the whole of you; the self within you is whole, held and never alone.
queries.act: Hold on through the dark night and reach out to someone who cares; the self within you is not broken and is never alone.

hook.speaker: Arjuna
hook.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
hook.sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाचअयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः । अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥
hook.line: What happens to someone who believes, tries, slips, and doesn't make it to the end?
hook.translation: Arjuna said: One who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind falls away from yoga before reaching perfection, what end does he come to, Krishna?
hook.why: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

prasang.title: What becomes of one who falls from yoga
prasang.summary: Arjuna fears that one who falls short is lost like a torn cloud. Krishna promises that no one who does good comes to ruin; past effort carries forward and they strive again.
prasang.lesson: No sincere effort is wasted; you pick up where you left off.

alternates.speaker: Rama
alternates.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
alternates.line: My heart feels heavy as stone, but I don't cry, because of what people would think.
alternates.translation: Though my heart is packed tight with the stones of life's sorrows, I don't let my tears fall, only out of fear of what my own people would think.
alternates.why: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.
alternates.misuse: Holding tears in is not strength. Rama's healing began when he finally said it aloud.

prasang.title: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.story_hook: In front of the whole court, the young prince stood up and said what everyone feels and nobody says.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

alternates.speaker: Rama
alternates.setting: Rama, ending his questions, asks for one practical skill.
alternates.sanskrit: व्यवहारवतो युक्त्या दुःखं नायाति मे यया । अथवा व्यवहारस्य ब्रूत तां युक्तिमुत्तमाम् ॥
alternates.line: Teach me how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow.
alternates.translation: Tell me the skill by which sorrow doesn't come to me while I go about my work, or else tell me the best way of dealing with life itself.
alternates.why: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

prasang.title: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasang.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasang.story_hook: Having said what was wrong, Rama finally asked the question that matters: how do the wise do it?
prasang.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: आशा नाम नदी मनोरथजला तृष्णातरङ्गाकुला रागग्राहवती वितर्कविहगा धैर्यद्रुमध्वंसिनी । मोहावर्तसुदुस्तरातिगहना प्रोत्तुङ्गचिन्तातटी तस्याः पारगता विशुद्धमनसो नन्दन्ति योगीश्वराः ॥
verse.line: Hope is a river: its water is wishes, its waves are craving, and its high banks are worry.
verse.translation: There is a river called Hope. Its water is wishes, its waves are craving; passions are its crocodiles, doubts its birds; it uproots the trees of courage; its whirlpools of delusion are hard to cross and deep, and its banks of worry tower high. Only great yogis, pure in mind, who reach the far shore, rejoice.
verse.why: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

prasang.title: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

why: The river called Hope (Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka 10)
Shows worry as part of one river fed by wishing

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', written to the Maharaja of Khetri.
verse.line: Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come.
verse.translation: If the sun by the cloud is hidden a bit, If the welkin shows but gloom, Still hold on yet a while, brave heart, The victory is sure to come. … Not a work will be lost, no struggle vain, Though hopes be blighted, powers gone; … Then hold on yet a while, brave soul, No good is e'er undone.
verse.why: No struggle is wasted; hold on a little longer.

matched.label: I can't handle not knowing what comes next

prasang.title: 'Hold on yet a while, brave heart' (poem to the Maharaja of Khetri)
prasang.summary: A short poem of encouragement to a friend. Clouds hide the sun for a while, summer always follows winter, and no honest struggle is wasted even when hopes fail.
prasang.lesson: No struggle is wasted; hold on a little longer.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

why: Weariness at unrewarded work is met by naming both possible ends
Failure is one of two normal outcomes, not a judgement

verse.speaker: Sanatkumara
verse.setting: A step in Sanatkumara's ladder: faith rests on steadiness, steadiness on action.
verse.sanskrit: यदा वै करोत्यथ निस्तिष्ठति नाकृत्वा निस्तिष्ठति कृत्वैव निस्तिष्ठति कृतिस्त्वेव विजिज्ञासितव्येति कृतिं भगवो विजिज्ञास इति ॥
verse.line: Steadiness comes from doing. No one becomes steady without acting; act, and steadiness follows.
verse.translation: When one acts, one becomes steadfast. One does not become steadfast without acting; only by acting does one become steadfast. So action itself must be understood. 'Sir, I wish to understand action.'
verse.why: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

prasang.title: Narada: learned but sad
prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.story_hook: Narada knew every subject worth knowing, and still came to Sanatkumara feeling sad.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

why: steadiness is built by the doing itself

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.line: hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
verse.translation: Never mind failures; they are quite natural, they are the beauty of life, these failures. What would life be without them? It would not be worth having if it were not for struggles. Where would be the poetry of life? Never mind the struggles, the mistakes. I never heard a cow tell a lie, but it is only a cow — never a man. So never mind these failures, these little backslidings; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
verse.why: Failure is part of the path; try once more.

prasang.title: Never mind failures (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Fill the mind with the highest thoughts. Failures are natural, even the beauty of life; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, try once more.
prasang.lesson: Failure is part of the path; try once more.

why: hold the ideal a thousand times

story.title: Markandeya and the child on the banyan leaf
story.story_hook: The whole world was one dark ocean, and on it floated a single banyan tree with a child asleep on a branch.
story.summary: At the end of an age, the sage Markandeya drifts alone over a flooded world and sees a radiant child on a banyan branch. The child draws him inside his body, where he sees all the worlds, then asks if he has been resting, tired. Narayana explains he showed himself because he saw Markandeya's distress. Markandeya tells the Pandavas that this child is Krishna, sitting with them.
story.lesson: When everything you knew is underwater, you have not been forgotten; you are being held.
story.hook_title: An old sage drifted alone over a drowned world, and found a child asleep on a leaf
story.teaser: An old sage drifted alone over a drowned world, and found a child asleep on a leaf
